Ein Programm, das immer dasselbe tut, is: A program that always does the same thing is dull. To calculate, remember things and react, it needs variables — named drawers with values in them. You give the drawer a name, put something in, and later take it out again by that name.
In Drachenhauch meldest du jede Variable: In Drachenhauch you declare every variable first. That is what the DIM command is for (from “dimension”, to set a measure). You state two things: what the variable is called, and what type it has — that is, what kind of value fits inside.
Die erste Zeile legt die Schublade „punk: The first line creates the drawer “punkte”, which takes whole numbers only. The second puts the number 100 into it — here the equals sign means “gets the value”, not “is equal to” in the mathematical sense. The third takes the value out again and prints it.
Anlegen (DIM) und Belegen (=) darfst du: Declaring (DIM) and assigning (=) may be kept apart or pulled together. But declare you must, before you use a variable — and that protects you from typos: if you later write “punke” by accident, Drachenhauch notices that no such drawer exists.
Drachenhauch kennt vier grundlegende Wer: Drachenhauch has four basic value types. Every variable has exactly one of them — this is the “Pascal-strict typing” you sometimes hear about. It sounds severe, but it is on your side: it catches a whole class of mistakes before they can happen.
Eine ganze Zahl – positiv, negativ oder: A whole number — positive, negative or zero, with no decimal places. For anything you count: score, lives, positions, loop counters.
Eine Kommazahl (Fließkommazahl). Für all: A decimal number (floating point). For anything that needs fractions: speeds, percentages, physics. The decimal separator is a point.
Eine Zeichenkette, also Text. Steht imme: A string of characters — text, in other words. Always in double quotes. Two strings can be joined with + (concatenated).
Ein Wahrheitswert: entweder TRUE (wahr): A truth value: either TRUE or FALSE. For yes/no states: is the game over? Is the door open? Essential for decisions (see the chapter on branching).
Weil jede Variable ihren Typ hat, kann D: Because every variable has its type, Drachenhauch can spot nonsense early. Putting a whole number into a FLOAT drawer is fine (3 becomes 3.0). But forcing text into a number drawer will not work — and that is just as well, because it would almost always be an accident.

Manche Werte ändern sich nie – die Breit: Some values never change — the width of the window, the acceleration of gravity, the name of your game. Those you declare as a constant with CONST. A constant gets its value once and may not be changed afterwards; try it anyway and Drachenhauch will object. That guards against overwriting something by accident, and makes the code easier to read.
Konstanten schreibt man oft in GROSSBUCH: Constants are often written in CAPITALS
Das ist nur Konvention, kein Zwang – abe: That is convention, not obligation — but it makes it immediately visible in the code that this value does not change.
Variablennamen beginnen mit einem Buchst: Variable names begin with a letter and may contain letters, digits and underscores. Upper and lower case make no difference: “punkte”, “Punkte” and “PUNKTE” all mean the same drawer. Above all, choose names that speak — “punkte” says more than “p”, and “spieler_x” more than “sx”. Your future self will thank you.
„step“ ist ein reserviertes Wort (es geh: “step” is a reserved word (it belongs to the FOR loop, see the chapter on loops). So call your counter i, schritt or tick — anything but step.
Ein Ausdruck ist alles, was zu einem Wer: An expression is anything that turns into a value: a number, a calculation, a comparison. Operators are the little symbols that join values together. You already know +, -, * and / from the first chapter — here is the whole toolbox.
Die vier Grundrechenarten funktionieren: The four basic operations work as you would expect. Two useful specialists for whole numbers come on top:
Addition, Subtraktion, Multiplikation, D: Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division. Division with / gives you a decimal number as soon as the sum does not come out even — 9 / 2 = 4.5, for instance. When it does come out even, you get a whole number (8 / 2 = 4).
Teilt und wirft den Rest weg – das Ergeb: Divides and throws the remainder away — the result is a whole number. Handy when decimal places are of no interest to you.
Liefert den Rest einer Division. 17 gete: Gives the remainder of a division. 17 divided by 5 is 3 remainder 2 — so 17 MOD 5 is 2. Indispensable for checking whether something “comes out even” (remainder 0), or for forcing values into a range.
Bei Strings bedeutet + nicht „addieren“,: With strings, + does not mean “add” but “join on the end”. That is how you build a sentence out of parts:
Vergleichs-Operatoren prüfen eine Behaup: Comparison operators test a claim and hand back a truth value (TRUE or FALSE). These are exactly the values that will steer your program's decisions later on.
kleiner, größer, kleiner-gleich, größer-: less than, greater than, less or equal, greater or equal
Zum Vergleichen nimmst du ein einzelnes: For comparing you use a single =. The same symbol is also used for assigning (punkte = 100). Drachenhauch tells from the context which is meant — in a condition = compares, in an assignment it assigns.
Mehrere Wahrheitswerte verknüpfst du mit: You combine several truth values with AND, OR and NOT. AND is true only when both sides are true; OR is true when at least one side is true; NOT turns a value around.
Drachenhauch hält sich an die gewohnten: Drachenhauch keeps to the usual precedence rules: arithmetic first (* and / before + and -), then comparison, then logic. If you want it otherwise — or simply want to be sure — you use brackets. Brackets are never wrong, and they make your intent plain:
Wer auf der Ebene einzelner Bits arbeite: If you want to work at the level of individual bits (for flags or masks, say), there are six operators: BAND (bitwise and), BOR (bitwise or), BXOR (bitwise exclusive or), SHL and SHR (shift left / right) and BNOT (flip the bits). They work strictly with whole numbers. If none of that means anything to you right now — no matter, you will rarely need them.
Bitweise Verknüpfungen ganzer Zahlen. Be: Bitwise operations on whole numbers. For example: 6 is 110 in binary, 3 is 011; the bitwise and gives 010, that is 2. SHL shifts the bits to the left — each place doubles the value.
Ein Programm, das nichts anzeigt und nic: A program that shows nothing and asks nothing would be a quiet affair. In this chapter you meet the two commands with which your program talks to the person in front of it: PRINT writes something to the screen, INPUT reads something from the keyboard. At the end, f-strings join in — an elegant way of weaving text and values into one sentence.
PRINT kennst du schon aus den ersten Kap: You already know PRINT from the first chapters. It outputs one or more values and then moves to the next line. You list values by stringing them together with a separator — and it is that separator which decides how the output looks.
Gibt die Werte aus und beginnt danach ei: Outputs the values and then starts a new line. Separate several values with a comma or a semicolon — see below. PRINT with no argument at all outputs a blank line.
Komma oder Semikolon – der feine Untersc: Comma or semicolon — the fine distinction
Beide Trennzeichen hängen die Werte hint: Both separators put the values one after another — but the comma inserts a space between them and the semicolon does not. That gives you precise control over the output:
trennt ohne Zwischenraum – die Werte kle: separates with no gap — the values run straight into each other.
Ein Semikolon am Zeilenende hat noch ein: A semicolon at the end of the line has one more special effect: it suppresses the line break. The next PRINT then carries straight on — handy for building up a line in several steps.
INPUT hält das Programm an, wartet auf e: INPUT halts the program, waits for the user to type something (finished with the Enter key) and puts what was typed into a variable. The neat part: Drachenhauch converts the input to the variable's type automatically. If that is an INTEGER variable, the typed text becomes a number; with STRING it stays text.
Liest eine Zeile von der Tastatur in die: Reads a line from the keyboard into the given variable. You may put a text in front as a question — it then appears before the input cursor. Without a text of your own, Drachenhauch simply shows “? ”. The variable must have been declared with DIM beforehand.
Weil die Variable den Typ vorgibt, kanns: Because the variable dictates the type, you can carry straight on calculating if you use a number variable:
Tippt der Benutzer bei einer INTEGER- od: If the user types something that is not a number into an INTEGER or FLOAT variable (“hallo”, say), Drachenhauch reports an error. To catch that, read into a STRING variable instead and convert the text gently with TRYVAL — there you can name a fallback value.
INPUT ist für Konsolen-Programme gedacht: INPUT is meant for console programs. In a graphical game with its own window you do not ask for input with INPUT; you read keyboard and mouse once per frame instead — you will learn that in Part IV (chapter “Input”).
Sätze aus Bausteinen mit + zusammenzuset: Assembling sentences from parts with + works, but it quickly becomes hard to read — quotation marks, plus signs and STR$ conversions everywhere. An f-string is nicer: you write a small f directly before the opening quote and put the values in curly braces { } in the middle of the text. Drachenhauch fills them in for you when it prints.
Ein String mit Platzhaltern. Was in gesc: A string with placeholders. Whatever stands inside curly braces is worked out as an expression and inserted at that spot. Anything may go in there: variables, calculations, even function calls.
Brauchst du eine echte geschweifte Klamm: If you need a real curly brace in the text, write it twice — {{ and }} become a single brace and are not read as a placeholder:
Manchmal soll eine Zahl in einer bestimm: Sometimes a number should appear in a particular shape: a decimal with exactly one place after the point, or a score padded with leading zeros. For that you append a colon and a format specification inside the placeholder — in the same style as FORMAT$, which comes next.
Dabei bedeutet .1f „Kommazahl mit einer: Here .1f means “decimal with one place after the point” and 05d means “whole number, at least 5 digits, padded with zeros at the front”. The FORMAT$ command understands the same specifications, in case you want to format outside an f-string:
Formatiert einen Wert nach einer Format-: Formats a value according to a C-style format specification and returns a string. Typical specifications: "%.2f" (two decimal places), "%05d" (number with leading zeros), "%x" (hexadecimal).
Für die meiste Ausgabe sind f-Strings di: For most output, f-strings are the pleasantest choice — they read almost like the finished sentence. Fall back on PRINT with comma or semicolon only when you want exact control over the spacing.
Bisher liefen unsere Programme stur von: So far our programs have run doggedly from top to bottom — line by line. It gets interesting when a program makes decisions: “if the hit points are zero, the game is over.” That is exactly what branching is for. It tests a condition and, depending on the result, runs different commands. In this chapter you meet IF, SELECT CASE and the compact one-liner IIF.
Ein IF prüft eine Bedingung – einen Ausd: An IF tests a condition — an expression that comes out TRUE or FALSE (you remember the comparison operators from the last chapter). If it is true, the block between THEN and END IF runs; if it is false, the block is skipped.
Führt den eingerückten Block nur aus, we: Runs the indented block only when the condition is true. The THEN sits at the end of the IF line, and END IF closes the block.
Oft willst du das eine ODER das andere t: Often you want to do one thing OR the other. With ELSE you give a second block, which runs precisely when the condition is false:
Manchmal gibt es nicht nur zwei Möglichk: Sometimes there are not just two possibilities but a whole staircase of cases. With ELSEIF you append further conditions. Drachenhauch tests them from top to bottom and takes the first block whose condition holds — the rest are skipped. A closing ELSE catches everything that has not matched so far.
Eine Kette von Bedingungen. Der erste pa: A chain of conditions. The first matching branch wins; ELSE is the catch-all branch for every remaining case. (ELIF is an accepted short form of ELSEIF.)
Die Reihenfolge zählt! Hier passt sowohl: Order matters! Here both “>= 75” and “>= 50” fit — but because 75 is tested first, “grade 2” wins. So arrange your conditions from the most specific to the most general.
Geht es nur um einen einzigen Befehl, da: When only a single command is involved, you may write the whole IF on one line — with no END IF. That keeps short tests brief and readable:
Beim einzeiligen IF folgt direkt nach TH: In a single-line IF the command to run follows directly after THEN — and there is NO END IF. As soon as you need several lines or an ELSE branch, use the full form with END IF.
Viele Fälle übersichtlich: SELECT CASE: Many cases, kept clear: SELECT CASE
Wenn du ein und denselben Wert gegen vie: When you test one and the same value against many possibilities, a long IF-ELSEIF staircase soon becomes hard to follow. SELECT CASE is made for exactly that: you name the value to be tested once, and list the cases underneath. The first matching CASE wins; CASE ELSE catches the rest.
Wertet den Ausdruck einmal aus und vergl: Evaluates the expression once and compares it against the CASE patterns in turn. A CASE may be a single value, a comma-separated list, or a range.
Bereiche und Vergleiche im CASE: Ranges and comparisons in a CASE
Ein CASE muss nicht auf exakte Werte war: A CASE need not wait for exact values. With TO you give a range (both bounds count), with IS a comparison. All the forms may be mixed as well, for instance CASE 1, 5 TO 8, IS > 100.
Der zu prüfende Wert wird nur ein einzig: The value being tested is worked out once only — even when it is an expensive function call. That is an advantage over an IF staircase, in which you would have to repeat the expression at every test.
Manchmal soll ein CASE nur greifen, wenn: Sometimes a CASE should only take effect when a further condition is met as well. For that you append WHERE. If the pattern fits but the WHERE expression is false, Drachenhauch tries the next CASE. That lets you combine the value with any additional knowledge:
Wäre trank hier FALSE, würde der „heilen: Were trank FALSE here, the “heal” case would not take effect and the next matching CASE (“flee”) would take over.
Die Entscheidung als Ausdruck: IIF: The decision as an expression: IIF
Bisher waren Verzweigungen ganze Anweisu: So far branches have been whole blocks of statements. Sometimes, though, you only want to pick between two values — a direction, a piece of text, a colour. That is what IIF (“inline if”) is for: it takes a condition and two values, and returns one or the other depending on the condition. IIF fits in the middle of an assignment or a PRINT.
Liefert den zweiten Wert, wenn die Bedin: Returns the second value when the condition is true, otherwise the third. Only the chosen branch is evaluated — the other side is not worked out at all (no division-by-zero mishap in the unused branch).
Nimm IIF, wenn du genau einen Wert auswä: Use IIF when you are picking exactly one value and want to use it straight away (dx = IIF(links, -speed, speed)). As soon as several commands should run per branch, the full IF ... END IF is the clearer choice.
Computer sind unermüdlich – und genau da: Computers are tireless — and loops are how we put that to use. A loop repeats a block of commands until some condition is met. Whether you are counting from 1 to 100, updating every enemy in a game, or rolling the dice until a six comes up: loops are the heart of almost every program. Drachenhauch has several kinds, each for a different situation.
Eine feste Anzahl: FOR ... NEXT: A fixed number of times: FOR ... NEXT
Die FOR-Schleife zählt eine Variable von: The FOR loop counts a variable up from a starting value to an end value and runs the block for each value. The NEXT marks the end of the block — that is where Drachenhauch jumps back and increases the counter.
Wiederholt den Block, während die Zählva: Repeats the block while the counter runs from start to end (both bounds included). After each pass the variable is increased by 1. The counter must have been declared with DIM beforehand.
Standardmäßig zählt FOR in Einerschritte: By default FOR counts upwards in steps of one. With STEP you give a different stride — a negative one as well, to count backwards:
STEP ist ein Schlüsselwort. Nenne deine: STEP is a keyword. So do not call your counter “step” — use i, j, zaehler or something that says what it means.
Solange eine Bedingung gilt: WHILE ... W: As long as a condition holds: WHILE ... WEND
Manchmal weißt du vorher nicht, wie oft: Sometimes you do not know in advance how often something has to be repeated — only under what condition. The WHILE loop tests its condition BEFORE each pass and runs as long as it is true. If it is already false at the start, the block does not run at all.
Wiederholt den Block, solange die Beding: Repeats the block as long as the condition is true. The test happens at the start of each pass. WEND closes the loop.
Achte darauf, dass sich in der Schleife: Make sure something changes inside the loop that eventually makes the condition false — otherwise the loop runs for ever and your program hangs. In the example n doubles each time and finally passes 100.
Die REPEAT-Schleife ist das Gegenstück z: The REPEAT loop is the counterpart to WHILE: it tests its condition only at the END. That guarantees the block runs at least once — ideal when you want to do something first and only then decide whether to repeat it (“roll until a three comes up”, say).
Wiederholt den Block, bis die Bedingung: Repeats the block until the condition becomes true. The test happens at the end — so the block always runs at least once.
Der Unterschied auf einen Blick: WHILE p: The difference at a glance: WHILE tests BEFORE (may never run), REPEAT tests AFTER (runs at least once). And mind the wording: WHILE runs as long as the condition is TRUE — REPEAT runs UNTIL it becomes true.
Sehr oft willst du nicht Zahlen hochzähl: Very often you do not want to count numbers up but to work through each element of a collection in turn — every name in a list, every letter of a word, every enemy in the game. FOR EACH is made for that: on each pass it hands you the next element directly.
Durchläuft jedes Element der Sammlung un: Walks through every element of the collection and puts it into var one after another. Works with tuples, arrays, the characters of a string and the keys of a map (you will meet those collections in the following chapters).
Zwei kleine Befehle geben dir mitten in: Two small commands hand control back to you in the middle of a loop. They work in all four kinds of loop:
bricht die Schleife sofort ganz ab und s: breaks off the loop entirely and jumps past the NEXT or WEND.
überspringt den Rest des aktuellen Durch: skips the rest of the current pass and carries straight on with the next one.
Hier überspringt CONTINUE alle geraden Z: Here CONTINUE skips all the even numbers, and as soon as i rises above 7, BREAK ends the loop — so only the odd numbers up to 7 are printed.
Du darfst Schleifen ineinander setzen. F: You may put loops inside one another. For every pass of the outer loop, the inner one runs through completely. That is how you build a grid, a small times table, or later draw a tile map row by row:
Kennst du die Anzahl der Durchläufe im V: If you know the number of passes in advance, use FOR. If you have a collection, use FOR EACH. If the repetition depends on a condition, use WHILE (tested before) or REPEAT (at least one pass).
Sobald ein Programm wächst, willst du di: As soon as a program grows, you do not want to write the same job out ten times. Functions and SUBs are named building blocks: you package a piece of work once, give it a name — and then call it as often as you like. That makes programs shorter, easier to read and easier to repair, because each piece of logic lives in exactly one place. This chapter shows everything Drachenhauch gives you for the purpose.
Eine FUNCTION nimmt Werte entgegen, rech: A FUNCTION takes values, works something out and hands back a result with RETURN. The type of the return value follows AS. You call it like a built-in command — and can use the result straight away.
Definiert eine Funktion mit Parametern u: Defines a function with parameters and a return type. RETURN delivers the result and ends the function immediately. The call name(...) becomes the value that was worked out.
Eine SUB ist eine Funktion ohne Rückgabe: A SUB is a function without a return value. It gets a job done — printing something, changing a state, writing a file — but it hands back no result to carry on with. You call it as a statement in its own right.
Definiert einen benannten Befehlsblock o: Defines a named block of commands with no return value. It is called as a statement of its own. A RETURN without a value can leave a SUB early.
Faustregel: Liefert der Baustein einen W: Rule of thumb: if the building block delivers a value you go on to use, take FUNCTION. If it simply does something, take SUB.
Du kannst beliebig viele Parameter angeb: You may give as many parameters as you like — separated by commas, each with its own type. When calling, you supply the values in the same order. Those values are called arguments.
Parameter sind lokal: Sie existieren nur: Parameters are local: they exist only inside the function. If you change them there, the value outside is untouched (except with BYREF — more on that in a moment). Functions also cannot see the caller's local variables; whatever they need, they receive as a parameter.
Normalerweise bekommt eine Funktion eine: Normally a function receives a copy of its arguments — changes to them stay inside. Put BYREF in front of a parameter and the function works directly on the variable that was passed in. An assignment then takes effect outside as well. That is how you return values without using RETURN.
Übergibt die Variable selbst statt einer: Passes the variable itself instead of a copy. Writes inside the function change the caller's variable. Only real variables can be passed BYREF, not fixed values such as 5.
Wenn du mehr als einen Wert zurückgeben: If you want to return more than one value, there is a more elegant way than BYREF: return a tuple and unpack it at the call site. You will learn that in the chapter “Tuples and destructuring”.
Einem Parameter kannst du einen Standard: You can give a parameter a default value. If the caller leaves that argument out, the default steps in. Handy for options that are mostly the same. Parameters with a default come at the end of the list.
Bei vielen oder ähnlichen Parametern ver: With many or similar parameters it is easy to lose track of which value belongs where. You may also name arguments when calling — then the order does not matter and the call reads for itself.
Manchmal weißt du nicht im Voraus, wie v: Sometimes you do not know in advance how many values will be passed. A parameter with three dots in front of it collects all the remaining arguments into a tuple. It must be the last one.
In Drachenhauch ist eine Funktion selbst: In Drachenhauch a function is itself a value, which you can store in a variable of type FUNCREF and call later. That lets you pass “what is to be done” as an argument — a comparison function for sorting, say, or a callback for an event.
Eine Variable, die auf eine Funktion ver: A variable that refers to a function. The bare function name (without brackets) becomes the reference; with f(...) you call the function behind it.
A function may call itself. That is called recursion, and it suits problems that break down into smaller versions of themselves — the factorial, for instance (5! = 5 · 4 · 3 · 2 · 1). What matters is a stopping case that ends the chain; without one the function calls itself for ever.
Jede Rekursion braucht einen Abbruchfall: Every recursion needs a stopping case that returns without calling itself again — here n <= 1. Without it the function goes deeper and deeper until the program stops with an error.
Gib Funktionen sprechende Namen (berechn: Give functions names that speak (berechne_schaden rather than bs), keep them short, and let each do exactly one thing. If you need a function in many places, move it into a file of its own and pull it in with IMPORT — you will learn that in the chapter “Importing modules”.
Ein String ist eine Zeichenkette – Text,: A string is a sequence of characters — text, enclosed in quotation marks. You have been using strings all along; here you get to know them properly: measuring their length, cutting pieces out, searching, replacing, splitting apart and putting back together. For almost every text job there is a suitable built-in command.
Viele String-Funktionen tragen ein $ am: Many string functions carry a $ at the end of the name (LEFT$, MID$, UPPER$ …). That is an old BASIC tradition, marking a function that returns a string. In Drachenhauch you may leave the $ off: UPPER$ and UPPER are the same thing.
Liefert die Anzahl der Zeichen in einem: Gives the number of characters in a string. (LEN works for arrays too, where it gives the number of elements.)
Wandelt den ganzen Text in Groß- bzw. Kl: Converts the whole text to upper or lower case. Handy for comparing input without having to care how it was capitalised.
Mit LEFT$ und RIGHT$ holst du dir die er: With LEFT$ and RIGHT$ you fetch the first or last characters. MID$ cuts from any position you like. Important: the position in MID$ is counted from 0 — the first character is at position 0, the second at position 1, and so on.
LEFT$ liefert die ersten n Zeichen, RIGH: LEFT$ gives the first n characters, RIGHT$ the last n.
Liefert ab der Position start (0-basiert: Gives up to n characters starting at position start (0-based!). Leave n out and it runs to the end of the string.
Anders als manche älteren BASIC-Dialekte: Unlike some older BASIC dialects, Drachenhauch counts character positions from 0, not from 1. The first character of "Drachenhauch" (the D) sits at position 0, the first h at position 4. The same holds for INSTR and for the index access further down.
Du kannst auf ein einzelnes Zeichen dire: You can reach a single character directly by its position — with square brackets, as with an array. With the colon notation you can even cut out a whole range (that is called slicing).
Beim Slicing wort[4:9] ist die untere Gr: When slicing, wort[4:9] includes the lower bound but not the upper one — you get positions 4 to 8. Either bound may be left out: wort[:4] is the first four characters, wort[4:] the rest from position 4 onwards.
Sucht teil$ in s$ und liefert dessen Pos: Looks for teil$ inside s$ and gives its position (counted from 0), or -1 if it does not occur. You may say which position to start searching from.
Willst du nur wissen, OB ein Text enthal: If you only want to know WHETHER a text occurs, CONTAINS or the IN operator are more convenient — both give a truth value:
Ersetzt alle Vorkommen von alt$ durch ne: Replaces every occurrence of alt$ with neu$ and gives back the new string.
Entfernt Leerzeichen (und andere Leerrau: Removes spaces (and other whitespace) at the beginning and end. Indispensable for user input, where a stray space likes to creep in. (LTRIM$ / RTRIM$ clean only the left or right side.)
SPLIT$ zerschneidet einen Text an einem: SPLIT$ cuts a text into its parts at a separator — the result is an array of strings (you will meet arrays in the next chapter). JOIN$ is the reverse: it puts the parts back together with a separator between them.
Füllt den String auf die gewünschte Brei: Pads the string out to the width you want — PADL$ on the left (right-aligned), PADR$ on the right (left-aligned). With no fill character, a space is used. Good for tables and leading zeros.
Hängt den String n-mal aneinander. Auch: Joins the string to itself n times. The star works for this too: "-" * 20 gives 20 hyphens.
Eine Zahl ist kein String – willst du si: A number is not a string — to build it into text you have to convert it (or use an f-string). The other way round, you turn typed text into a number you can calculate with.
STR$ wandelt eine Zahl in ihren Text um,: STR$ turns a number into its text, VAL turns a text into a number. If the text cannot be read as a number, VAL gives 0 — with TRYVAL(s, ersatz) you can name a fallback value of your own instead.
CHR$ macht aus einer Zeichen-Nummer (dem: CHR$ turns a character number (the Unicode code point) into the character itself; ASC does the reverse, giving the number of the first character. A is 65, B is 66, and so on.
Viele dieser Funktionen kannst du wahlwe: Many of these functions can also be hung on the string in dot notation — that often reads more fluently, and can be chained:
Für das Zusammensetzen von Text aus Wert: For assembling text out of values, an f-string is usually the pleasantest choice: f"{name} hat {punkte} Punkte" saves you all those + signs and STR$ calls. See the chapter “Input and output”.
Bisher hatte jede Variable genau einen W: So far every variable has held exactly one value. But often many values belong together: the scores of all the players, the hit points of every enemy, the tiles of a game map. Making a separate variable for each (gegner1, gegner2, gegner3 …) would be tedious and inflexible. An array solves that: it is a single variable that gathers many values under one name — numbered and lined up in order.
Stell dir ein Array wie eine Reihe numme: Picture an array as a row of numbered lockers. They all carry the same name (punkte, say), but each has a number of its own. Through that number — the index — you address a single locker. That way a loop can run effortlessly over hundreds or thousands of values without your ever having to invent a new variable name.
Ein Array deklarierst du mit DIM – wie e: You declare an array with DIM — like an ordinary variable, but with the number of lockers in square brackets. The type each locker takes follows AS. Freshly created, every locker holds the default value: 0 for numbers, the empty text for strings, FALSE for truth values.
Legt ein Array mit der angegebenen Anzah: Creates an array with the given number of lockers, all of the named type and pre-filled with its default value. The count goes in square brackets.
Ein einzelnes Fach sprichst du über sein: You address a single locker by its index in square brackets. And here comes the single most important point: counting starts at 0, not at 1. An array with 5 lockers therefore has the valid indices 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 — the last locker carries the number 4, not 5.
Das fühlt sich am Anfang ungewohnt an, i: That feels odd at first, but it is how nearly all modern programming languages work. Remember it like this: the index is the “distance from the start”. The first element is zero steps from the start, hence index 0.
Greifst du auf ein Fach zu, das es nicht: If you reach for a locker that does not exist — punkte[5] with only 5 lockers, say (0 to 4 are valid) — the program stops with an error. Always take care to stay inside the bounds. LEN tells you where the bound is (see below).
Ein Array gleich mit Werten füllen: das: Filling an array right away: the array literal
Jedes Fach einzeln zu beschreiben ist um: Writing to every locker one at a time is cumbersome when you already know the values. That is what the array literal is for: a list of values in square brackets, separated by commas. With it you create a ready-filled array in a single line. Drachenhauch works out the type of the lockers from the values themselves.
Erzeugt ein fertig gefülltes Array. Nur: Creates a ready-filled array. Whole numbers only give an INTEGER array, decimals a FLOAT array, texts a STRING array. The length is the number of values.
Ein Array-Literal kannst du überall eins: You can use an array literal anywhere an array is expected — even directly in a loop, without assigning it to a variable first:
Ein leeres Array-Literal [] ist nicht er: An empty array literal [] is not allowed — with no values the type could not be worked out. For an empty array that you fill gradually, use DIM name[0] AS Typ (see “Arrays that grow and shrink” further down). And take care: [x FOR x IN …] with the keyword FOR is NOT an array literal but a “comprehension” — a different tool, which you will meet in a later chapter.
LEN sagt dir, wie viele Elemente ein Arr: LEN tells you how many elements an array has. You will need that constantly — above all to run a loop safely over every locker. Because the indices start at 0, the loop runs from 0 to LEN minus 1.
Liefert die Anzahl der Elemente eines Ar: Gives the number of elements in an array. (For multi-dimensional arrays, the size of the first dimension.)
Geht es dir nur um die Werte und nicht u: If it is only the values you care about and not the indices, FOR EACH is shorter still — it hands you each element directly, with no juggling of LEN and index:
Für die häufigsten Aufgaben gibt es fert: For the most common jobs there are ready-made commands. Important: SORT and REVERSE change the array on the spot (“in place”, as it is called) — they do not give back a new array but turn the existing one around.
SORT ordnet ein eindimensionales Array a: SORT puts a one-dimensional array into ascending order, REVERSE turns the order around. Both act directly on the array passed in. (SORT can also sort descending or work with a comparison function of your own — more on that later.)
Sucht den ersten Index, an dem wert steh: Finds the first index at which wert appears and gives it back — or -1 if the value does not occur.
Rechnen über das ganze Array: Aggregate: Calculating over the whole array: aggregates
Für Arrays aus Zahlen gibt es Befehle, d: For arrays of numbers there are commands that evaluate the whole array at once — sum, average, smallest and largest value. They save you the loop for these standard questions.
Liefern Summe, Durchschnitt, kleinstes u: Give the sum, average, smallest and largest element of a numeric array. ARRAY_AVG always comes out as a decimal; the array must not be empty for the average.
Setzt alle Fächer auf denselben Wert – p: Sets every locker to the same value — handy for resetting an array.
Bisher hatten unsere Arrays eine feste G: So far our arrays have had a fixed size. Often, though, you do not know in advance how many values will accumulate — a list of the bullets currently in flight, say, which grows and shrinks all the time. For that you can use an array dynamically: you create it empty (with 0 lockers) and append elements as needed.
Diese Befehle verändern das Array direkt: These commands change the array directly. ARRAY_PUSH appends at the end, ARRAY_POP takes the last one off again — together they make a stack, like a pile of plates on which you add at the top and take from the top.
ARRAY_PUSH hängt einen Wert hinten an un: ARRAY_PUSH appends a value at the end and gives the new length. ARRAY_POP removes the last element and gives it back (the array must not be empty for that).
ARRAY_INSERT schiebt einen Wert an Posit: ARRAY_INSERT pushes a value in at position idx (everything behind moves back); idx may run from 0 up to the length. ARRAY_REMOVE_AT removes the element at idx and gives it back (the rest moves forward).
REDIM(arr, länge) ändert die Größe eines: REDIM(arr, länge) changes an array's size after the fact: it grows (new lockers get the default value) or shrinks (surplus lockers fall away). Existing values are kept.
Wie bei Strings kannst du mit der Doppel: As with strings, the colon notation copies a section of an array. The lower bound is included, the upper one is not. Important: the result is a copy in its own right — changes to it do not touch the original array.
Hier lauert ein klassischer Stolperstein: A classic pitfall lurks here, and it is worth understanding properly. If you write b = a, NO copy of the array is made. Instead both names then point at the same array — as though one locker had two name plates on it. Change something through b and a changes too, because it is the same array.
KEINE Kopie – b und a sind dasselbe Arra: NOT a copy - b and a are the same array!
Willst du wirklich eine unabhängige Kopi: If you really want an independent copy — one you can change without touching the original — use ARRAY_COPY (or a slice such as a[:], which copies as well):
Liefert eine unabhängige Kopie des Array: Gives an independent copy of the array with the same shape and the same type. Changes to the copy leave the original untouched.
Ein Array kann auch ein Raster sein – et: An array can also be a grid — a chessboard or a game map, for instance. For that you give several sizes, separated by commas. You then address an element with as many indices. Picture it as a table with rows and columns.
Legt ein Raster an. Jedes Element wird m: Creates a grid. Every element is addressed with as many indices as there are dimensions. DIMCOUNT gives the number of dimensions, DIMSIZE(arr, n) the size of the nth.
Über ein zweidimensionales Array läufst: You walk over a two-dimensional array with two nested loops — the outer over the rows, the inner over the columns. This is exactly the pattern you will need later to draw a tile map or a playing field.
Ein Array nummeriert seine Werte mit gan: An array numbers its values with whole numbers from 0 — ideal when order matters or you walk through in sequence. If you need named keys instead ("spieler1" → 42), a map is the better choice. You will meet it in the next chapter.

An array numbers its values with whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, … That is perfect as long as position is the natural way in. But sometimes you want to address values not by a number but by a name: the score of “Anna”, the stock of “Holz”, the setting “lautstärke”. That is precisely what the map is for.
Eine Map ist eine Sammlung von Paaren au: A map is a collection of key-and-value pairs. Picture it as a dictionary: you look up a headword (the key) and get the explanation that goes with it (the value). Or as a telephone book — look up the name, get the number. The key replaces the array's index number with something that speaks.
In Drachenhauch sind die Schlüssel einer: In Drachenhauch the keys of a map are ALWAYS strings. The values, by contrast, have whatever type you state at DIM — MAP OF INTEGER stores numbers, MAP OF STRING stores texts, and so on.
Deklariert wird eine Map mit DIM ... AS: A map is declared with DIM ... AS MAP OF Typ. Freshly created it is empty. With MAPPUT you store a pair: you name the key and the value. If the key already exists, its old value is overwritten — so every key occurs only once.
Legt unter dem Schlüssel einen Wert ab o: Stores a value under the key, or overwrites the existing one. The key is a string; the value has the map's type.
Mit MAPGET holst du den Wert zu einem Sc: With MAPGET you fetch the value for a key. Here you have to take care: ask for a key that does not exist and MAPGET stops with an error. That is deliberate — a missing key at this point is usually a genuine bug that you want to notice at once.
Liefert den Wert zum Schlüssel. Existier: Gives the value for the key. If the key does not exist, an error is raised — when in doubt, check first with MAPHAS or use MAPGETOR.
Damit dir ein fehlender Schlüssel nicht: So that a missing key does not shoot your program down, there are two safe routes. MAPHAS checks whether a key is present at all. And MAPGETOR gives a fallback value of your own choosing if the key is missing — very handy for defaults.
Liefert TRUE, wenn der Schlüssel in der: Gives TRUE when the key is present in the map, otherwise FALSE. The IN operator does the same: schlüssel$ IN m.
Liefert den Wert zum Schlüssel – oder de: Gives the value for the key — or the fallback value if the key is missing. Never stops with an error.
MAPSIZE liefert die Anzahl der Paare. MA: MAPSIZE gives the number of pairs. MAPREMOVE deletes a pair and returns TRUE if the key was there. MAPCLEAR empties the whole map.
Oft willst du jedes Paar einer Map nache: Often you want to work through each pair of a map in turn — printing a league table, say. There are several ways to do it. The most direct is FOR EACH over the map: the loop variable then receives each KEY one after another, and MAPGET fetches the matching value.
Die Paare erscheinen in der Reihenfolge,: The pairs appear in the order in which you inserted them — first inserted, first out. You can rely on that.
Brauchst du die Schlüssel als Array (etw: If you need the keys as an array (to sort them, for instance), MAPKEYS gives them to you. MAPVALUES correspondingly gives all the values, and MAPITEMS all the pairs as little two-part bundles (tuples) of key and value:
MAPKEYS liefert ein Array aller Schlüsse: MAPKEYS gives an array of all the keys, MAPVALUES an array of all the values, MAPITEMS an array of (key, value) tuples. All in insertion order.
In paar[0] steckt jeweils der Schlüssel,: paar[0] holds the key and paar[1] the value — the two halves of the pair.
Wie bei Strings gibt es die meisten Map-: As with strings, most map commands also exist in dot notation, hung directly on the map. Which form you use is a matter of taste — they do the same thing.
Was, wenn der Schlüssel eine Zahl ist?: What if the key is a number?
Map-Schlüssel müssen Strings sein. Wills: Map keys must be strings. If you nevertheless want to look up by a number — caching a value per player number, say — simply convert the number to a string with STR$. That is a common pattern, for instance in a cache that remembers results already worked out so they need not be computed twice:
Wie ein Array ist eine Map ein Verweis-W: Like an array, a map is a reference value: write b = a and both names then point at the SAME map — a change through b takes effect on a as well. That is the same pitfall as with arrays (see the chapter “Arrays”). If you need a real copy, build it afresh with a loop over MAPITEMS.
Frag dich, wie du an deine Werte heran w: Ask yourself how you want to get at your values. By a running number and in a fixed order? -> array. By a name that speaks? -> map. The two can be combined, by the way: a MAP OF (ARRAY …) or an array of maps is perfectly fine.
Ein Tupel ist ein festes Bündel aus mehr: A tuple is a fixed bundle of several values that belong together — the x and y coordinate of a point, say, or a name together with an age. You simply write the values in round brackets, separated by commas. Unlike an array, a tuple may hold values of different types, and it has a fixed size that never changes.
Tupel glänzen vor allem in zwei Situatio: Tuples shine in two situations above all: they let a function return several results at once, and they can be elegantly taken apart into individual variables when assigned. That taking-apart is called destructuring — and it is the real star of this chapter.
Ein Tupel-Literal ist eine Liste von min: A tuple literal is a list of at least two values in round brackets. You store it in a variable of type TUPLE. You reach the individual values by index, as with an array (counted from 0 here too), and length() tells you how many there are.
Bündelt zwei oder mehr Werte – auch unte: Bundles two or more values — of different types as well — into a tuple. A single bracket such as (5) is NOT a tuple but merely a number in brackets; a tuple needs at least two elements.
Dass verschiedene Typen erlaubt sind, ma: Being allowed to mix types makes tuples ideal for gathering a small record together — here a name, an age and a truth value in a single value:
Ein wichtiger Unterschied zum Array: Ein: An important difference from the array: once created, a tuple cannot be changed. There is no assigning to a single slot — the attempt is refused. A tuple is a fixed snapshot. If you want different values, you build a new tuple.
FEHLER: ein Tupel lässt sich nicht änder: ERROR: a tuple cannot be changed
Genau diese Unveränderlichkeit macht Tup: It is precisely this immutability that makes tuples safe and easy to follow: when you pass a tuple somewhere, nobody can change it behind your back. If you need a changeable collection of like things, take an array (chapter “Arrays”).
Jetzt zum eigentlichen Trick. Statt die: Now for the real trick. Instead of laboriously pulling the individual values out via punkt[0], punkt[1], you can spread a tuple across several variables in one go. To do so you write brackets with the target variables on the left-hand side of the assignment. Drachenhauch unpacks the tuple and fills them in order.
Verteilt die Elemente eines Tupels auf m: Spreads the elements of a tuple across several variables. The number of variables on the left must match the number of tuple elements on the right exactly — otherwise you get an error.
Links müssen genau so viele Variablen st: There must be exactly as many variables on the left as the tuple has elements. Write (a, b) = (1, 2, 3) and the program stops with a clear message: “2 targets, but tuple has 3 element(s)”.
Hier zeigt sich die wahre Stärke. Eine F: This is where the real strength shows. A function can normally deliver only one value with RETURN. Pack several values into a tuple and you are effectively returning several results — and you take them apart again straight away at the call site. That is far more pleasant than the detour via BYREF from the functions chapter.
Will man die Werte zweier Variablen vert: To swap the values of two variables you classically need a third helper variable (remember x, overwrite x with y, write what you remembered into y). With destructuring it takes a single line — the right-hand side is worked out completely before anything is assigned:
Wie Arrays und Maps lässt sich auch ein: Like arrays and maps, a tuple can be walked with FOR EACH — handy for a short, fixed list that you do not want to put into an array first:
Nimm ein Tupel für ein kleines, festes B: Take a tuple for a small, fixed bundle of values that belong together — especially for returning several results, or for mixed types. Take an array for a larger collection of like things that should grow, shrink and change.
Bis hierhin hast du mit einzelnen Werten: Up to here you have worked with individual values — numbers, strings, arrays. But in a game many things belong closely together: an enemy has a position, hit points, a name and a behaviour. Managing that data in loosely adjacent variables (gegner_x, gegner_y, gegner_hp …) soon becomes unmanageable — all the more so when there are many enemies.
Die objektorientierte Programmierung bie: Object-oriented programming offers a tidier idea: you gather the data that belongs together AND the activities that go with it into a single structure — a class. This chapter leads you there step by step. Take your time; the concept is powerful and unfamiliar at first, but once the penny drops you will not want to be without it.
Bauplan und Objekt – der zentrale Gedank: Blueprint and object — the central idea
Stell dir eine Klasse wie einen Bauplan: Picture a class as a blueprint — the blueprint for a house, say. The plan itself is not a house; it merely describes what a house should look like: how many rooms it has, what colour, which doors. From ONE plan you can build as many real houses as you like, and each is a thing in its own right with its own values.
Genauso ist es hier: Die Klasse ist der: It is exactly the same here: the class is the blueprint, and the finished thing is called an object (or an instance). You write the class once and then create as many objects from it as you need — every enemy an object of its own, with its own hit points, but all built to the same plan.
= der Bauplan. Beschreibt, welche Daten: = the blueprint. Describes what data (fields) and what activities (methods) an object has.
= ein konkretes, aus dem Plan gebautes E: = a concrete specimen built from the plan, with values of its own.
Eine Klasse schreibst du zwischen CLASS: You write a class between CLASS and END CLASS. Inside come its fields first — variables that every object owns for itself. You declare them with DIM as usual. Here is a simple player with a name and hit points:
Das allein erzeugt noch nichts – es besc: That on its own creates nothing yet — it merely describes the blueprint. Every player built will have a name field and an hp field of its own.
Aus dem Bauplan baust du ein echtes Obje: From the blueprint you build a real object with the keyword NEW. You store the result in a variable whose type is the class name. Freshly built, the fields carry their default values (0 for numbers, the empty text for strings).
Den Punkt kennst du schon von den Method: You already know the dot from the methods on strings and maps. With objects it leads you to a field (held.hp) or straight to an activity (held.NimmSchaden(...), see below).
Es ist mühsam, nach jedem NEW alle Felde: Setting every field by hand after each NEW is tedious. For that there is a special building block: a SUB named Init. It runs automatically as soon as you create an object with NEW — and you give its arguments right there at the NEW. It is called the constructor (“the builder”).
In der Init-Methode (und in allen Method: In the Init method (and in every method) you need a way of addressing “the object being built right now”. That is what the keyword Self is for — it always means “this object here, the one I am working on”. So Self.hp = 100 sets the hp field of precisely this one object.
Self verweist immer auf das Objekt, für: Self always refers to the object the method is currently running for. Call held.NimmSchaden(...) and inside the method Self is the held; call gegner.NimmSchaden(...) and Self is the gegner. That way the same method code works on each object's own data.
Bis jetzt hat unsere Klasse nur Daten. D: So far our class has only data. The genuinely interesting part is methods: functions and SUBs that sit INSIDE the class and work on its fields. You define a method exactly like an ordinary SUB or FUNCTION (chapter “Functions and SUBs”) — just inside the class body, and with access to Self.
Erweitern wir den Spieler um Verhalten:: Let us extend the player with behaviour: take damage, check whether he is still alive, print his status.
Jetzt kannst du dem Objekt Befehle geben: Now you can give the object commands by calling the method with the dot. It reads almost like a sentence: “held, take 30 damage.”
Innerhalb einer Methode darfst du eine a: Inside a method you may call another method of the same class without Self. as well — a bare Reset() will do, and means the same as Self.Reset(). Both are allowed; the Self. simply makes it especially plain that this is a method of the object itself.
Der ganze Sinn eines Bauplans ist, dass: The whole point of a blueprint is that you build many independent objects from it. Each has its own set of fields — change one and the other is untouched. That is how you effortlessly manage a whole crowd of players or enemies, all with the same class:
Ein Objekt ist – wie Array und Map – ein: An object is a reference value, like an array or a map. Write zweiterHeld = held and NO copy is made: both names point at the same object, and a change through one takes effect on the other. If you want a genuine second player, build him with a NEW of his own.
Eine Klasse lohnt sich, sobald mehrere D: A class pays off as soon as several pieces of data belong together and there are activities that work on them — a player, an enemy, an item, a playing card. Rule of thumb: if you catch yourself writing variable names with the same prefix (spieler_x, spieler_y, spieler_hp), that is almost always a class calling. The next chapter carries on with inheritance, properties, operators and static members.
Vererbung, Properties, Operatoren & Stat: Inheritance, properties, operators and static members
Im letzten Kapitel hast du Klassen und O: In the last chapter you met classes and objects. Now four advanced tools join them, the ones that make the class system genuinely powerful: inheritance (classes building on others), properties (controlled access to fields), operator overloading (joining your own types with + and =) and static members (values belonging to the class itself). Each is a topic of its own — take them one at a time.
Oft sind sich mehrere Klassen ähnlich: E: Often several classes resemble one another: a dog and a cat are both animals — they have a name and can make a sound, but differ in the detail. Rather than writing everything twice, you define a general base class (Tier) and derive more specialised classes from it. The derived class inherits all the base's fields and methods, and can add its own.
Abgeleitet wird mit dem Schlüsselwort EX: Deriving is done with the keyword EXTENDS. One says: Hund is a subclass of Tier, and Tier is the superclass. A Hund therefore automatically has everything a Tier has.
Derives one class from another. The subclass inherits its fields and methods and may add its own. You reach inherited fields through Self just the same.
erbt name, Init und Beschreibung von Tie: inherits name, Init and Beschreibung from Tier
Eine Unterklasse kann eine geerbte Metho: A subclass can redefine an inherited method — that is called overriding. For its own objects it thereby replaces the superclass version. So every animal makes a sound in its own way, even though the method is called Sprich everywhere.
Überschreibt eine Unterklasse die Init-M: If a subclass overrides the Init method, the superclass Init is NOT called in addition automatically — the new Init replaces it entirely. Set the inherited fields yourself in your own Init, then. If you have no need to change the parent's preparation, simply define no Init of your own and the inherited one runs.
Hier wird Vererbung erst richtig nützlic: This is where inheritance really becomes useful. A variable of the superclass type may hold objects of the subclasses as well — a dog is, after all, an animal. When you then call a method, the version belonging to the actual object runs automatically. This “the right code is chosen at run time” is called polymorphism (many-shapedness).
Das erlaubt dir, ganz verschiedene Objek: That lets you treat quite different objects alike — walking through all the creatures in a list, say, and simply telling each one Sprich(), without knowing whether it is a dog or a cat:
Manchmal willst du nicht, dass jeder Cod: Sometimes you do not want every piece of code to change a field directly and unchecked. For example: the hit points should never fall below 0 or rise above 100. From the outside a property looks like an ordinary field (you write objekt.hp = 200), but on reading and writing it quietly runs your code — a guard that can check, limit or convert.
Dazu schreibst du zwei besondere Blöcke:: For that you write two special blocks: PROPERTY GET supplies the value when reading, PROPERTY SET receives it when writing (the assigned value is in value). The actual field is customarily hidden behind a name with an underscore, such as _hp.
Definiert kontrollierten Lese- und Schre: Defines controlled read and write access. GET runs when reading objekt.name, SET when assigning objekt.name = ... (the new value arrives as value). Define only GET and the property is read-only; only SET makes it write-only.
Für eigene Klassen, die mathematische We: For classes of your own that represent mathematical values — sums of money, vectors, fractions — you can lay down what +, -, =, < and so on mean between two objects. That is called operator overloading. Instead of geld_a.Plus(geld_b) you then simply write geld_a + geld_b — far more natural.
Dazu definierst du im Klassen-Body einen: For that you define an OPERATOR block in the class body: like a method, but with the operator symbol where the name would be. It takes exactly one parameter (the right-hand operand) and a return type.
Legt fest, wie ein Operator zwischen Obj: Lays down how an operator acts between objects of this class. Allowed are +, -, *, /, MOD, =, <>, <, >, <=, >=. The single parameter is the right-hand operand; Self is the left.
Pro Operator gibt es genau eine Definiti: There is exactly one definition per operator — mixing Geld + Geld and Geld + INTEGER in two separate blocks is not possible. Overloaded operators are inherited like methods. For ready-made mathematical types, by the way, Drachenhauch already ships modules, such as vec2 for 2D vectors (Part V).
Statische Mitglieder: zur Klasse, nicht: Static members: to the class, not the object
So far every field has belonged to an object. But some values belong to the class as a whole — fixed figures that are the same for every object and need no object to look them up: the maximum hit points, the game's name, gravity. That is what STATIC CONST is for. You address them through the class name, without ever creating an object.
Definiert eine zur Klasse gehörende Kons: Defines a constant belonging to the class, retrievable as Klassenname.NAME. The value must be a fixed literal (number, string, truth value). That gathers fixed figures tidily with their class instead of in loose global constants.
Innerhalb einer Methode der Klasse greif: Inside a method of the class you reach them the same way (Config.MAX_HP). Static constants are fixed — they cannot be overwritten at run time. If you need changeable, shared state, use a global variable instead.
Vererbung, Properties und Operatoren sin: Inheritance, properties and operators are strong tools — but not every program needs them. Do start with plain classes of fields and methods (chapter 20). Reach for inheritance when there are genuine “is a” relationships (a dog IS an animal), for properties where values have rules, for operators only with real arithmetic types. Clarity beats cleverness.
Programme stecken voller Zustände und Ka: Programs are full of states and categories: a game is in the menu, running, or paused. You could represent such cases with numbers (0 = menu, 1 = running, 2 = paused) — but who remembers that 2 means paused? An ENUM (short for “enumeration”) gives those numbers names that speak. Your code becomes readable and unmistakable as a result.
Im einfachsten Fall zählst du die Namen: In the simplest case you list the names compactly on one line. Drachenhauch hands out the numbers 0, 1, 2 and so on automatically. The values are addressed through the ENUM name with a dot — Status.MENU, that is. This notation makes it plain at once what is meant.
Definiert eine Aufzählung. Die Mitgliede: Defines an enumeration. The members receive the values 0, 1, 2, … in order and are addressed as Name.MITGLIED.
Brauchst du bestimmte Zahlen – etwa weil: If you need particular numbers — because they have to match data from outside, say — write the ENUM as a block and give each member its value. That stays readable once there are more entries.
Block-Schreibweise mit ausdrücklichen We: Block notation with explicit values. If you leave a member's value out, Drachenhauch counts on by one from the last value handed out.
Du darfst beide Stile mischen: Nach eine: You may mix the two styles: after an explicitly set value, the automatic numbering carries on from there. So in the following ENUM A is 0, B is set to 5, and C accordingly gets 6:
Eine Variable, die einen ENUM-Wert halte: A variable meant to hold an ENUM value is declared with the ENUM name as its type (internally it is a whole number). ENUMs go particularly well with SELECT CASE: the cases carry names that speak, and you can see at a glance that every state is covered.
Die Mitglieds-Namen dürfen sogar mit Sch: The member names may even coincide with keywords (READ, DATA, NEW …). Because they always stand behind the ENUM name and a dot (Befehl.READ), it is unambiguous that no command is meant.
Beide ersetzen „magische Zahlen“ durch N: Both replace “magic numbers” with names. Take an ENUM for a related group of mutually exclusive possibilities (the game states, the points of the compass). A STATIC CONST (chapter 21) suits a single fixed figure belonging to a particular class better.
Sehr oft will man aus einer vorhandenen: Very often one wants to build a new collection out of an existing one: from a list of numbers, the list of their squares; from all the players, only those with enough points. That can of course be done with a loop. Comprehensions are a shorter, very readable shorthand for exactly that pattern — “take every element and do something with it” — all on a single line.
Der Begriff klingt sperrig, die Idee ist: The term sounds unwieldy; the idea is simple. Read a comprehension like a sentence: “make n times n, for every n in zahlen.” That is exactly the order in which it is written.
Die Grundform steht in eckigen Klammern: The basic form sits in square brackets and has two parts: at the front the expression to be worked out for each element, behind it the FOR that walks the collection. The result is a tuple of all the computed values (you know tuples from chapter 19 — they cannot be changed).
Berechnet den Ausdruck für jedes Element: Works out the expression for every element of the collection and gathers the results into a tuple. Tuples, arrays, the characters of a string or the keys of a map can serve as the collection.
Vergleiche das mit der ausgeschriebenen: Compare that with the loop written out — both do the same thing, but the comprehension puts it on one line:
dieselbe Aufgabe mit einer Schleife:: the same job with a loop:
Hängst du ein WHERE samt Bedingung an, l: Append a WHERE with a condition and only those elements for which the condition is true end up in the result — the others are skipped. That way you filter and transform in one go. Here only the even numbers remain:
Wie die List-Comprehension, übernimmt ab: Like the list comprehension, but takes only the elements for which the condition holds.
Der Ausdruck vorne darf alles sein – ein: The expression at the front may be anything — a calculation, a function call, a method call. That is how you turn every character of a string into a capital, for instance:
Mit geschweiften Klammern und einem Dopp: With curly braces and a colon you build a whole map in one sweep. The key goes before the colon, the value behind it — both are worked out for every element. Remember: map keys are always strings (chapter 18), so convert with STR$ where needed.
Erzeugt eine Map, indem für jedes Elemen: Creates a map by working out a key-value pair for every element. A WHERE filter is allowed here too.
Schreibst du geschweifte Klammern OHNE D: Write curly braces WITHOUT a colon and you get a set comprehension. Like a list comprehension it works out one value per element, but it leaves duplicates out — every value appears only once, in the order of its first appearance. The result is a tuple again.
Wie die List-Comprehension, entfernt abe: Like the list comprehension, but removes duplicates. Handy for pulling the distinct values out of many.
Obwohl neun Zahlen hineingehen, kommen n: Although nine numbers go in, only three different remainders come out (0, 1, 2) — the repetitions were swallowed.
Wann Comprehension, wann Schleife?: When a comprehension, when a loop?
Eine Comprehension glänzt, wenn du aus e: A comprehension shines when you simply derive one collection from another — mapping and/or filtering. Once the logic grows more complicated (several steps, intermediate values, many conditions), the loop written out stays clearer. Readability before brevity.
Manche Dinge können schiefgehen, ohne da: Some things can go wrong without your being at fault as the programmer: a file is missing, an input makes no sense, a calculation accidentally divides by zero. When such a run-time error occurs, Drachenhauch normally stops the program with a message. Often, though, you do not want to crash but to catch the error cleanly and carry on. That is exactly what TRY, CATCH and THROW are for.
Du legst den heiklen Code in einen TRY-B: You put the delicate code into a TRY block. If all goes well it runs through as usual and the CATCH part is skipped. But if an error occurs anywhere in the TRY block, Drachenhauch jumps straight into the CATCH block — the rest of the TRY block is skipped, but the program is NOT stopped. Afterwards it carries on quite normally past END TRY.
Im CATCH kannst du eine Variable angeben: In the CATCH you may name a variable (here e). It then holds the error message as text — useful for seeing what happened.
Führt den TRY-Block aus. Tritt ein Fehle: Runs the TRY block. If an error occurs, the CATCH block runs instead. The optional variable after CATCH receives the error message as a string. After END TRY the program carries on normally — a caught error does not end it.
Beachte: Die Zeile nach der Division wur: Note: the line after the division was never executed — the moment the error occurred, execution jumped straight into the CATCH. But the program carried on afterwards and printed “weiter geht's” instead of crashing.
Eigene Fehler auslösen mit THROW: Raising your own errors with THROW
Du kannst Fehler auch selbst auslösen –: You can also raise errors yourself — when a value is not permissible, for instance. THROW throws an error with a message of your choosing. It behaves like a built-in run-time error: it breaks off the current flow and is caught by the nearest enclosing CATCH (across function calls as well).
Löst einen Fehler mit dem angegebenen We: Raises an error with the given value (usually a string). The flow breaks off and jumps to the nearest enclosing CATCH — no matter how many function calls lie in between.
Schön zu sehen: pruefe(25) lief normal d: Nicely visible: pruefe(25) ran through normally, pruefe(-5) threw the error. It jumped out of the SUB all the way to the CATCH in the calling code — that is how you cleanly separate spotting a problem (in the SUB) from dealing with it (in the CATCH).
Die Variable nach CATCH ist optional. In: The variable after CATCH is optional. If the exact message is of no interest to you, simply write CATCH with no name — the block still catches the error.
Wann (und wann nicht) Fehlerbehandlung?: When (and when not) to handle errors
TRY/CATCH ist mächtig, aber kein Ersatz: TRY/CATCH is powerful, but no substitute for ordinary branching. Use it for things that are REALLY exceptional and that you cannot simply check for beforehand — a missing file, broken user input, a network problem. For normal decisions (“does the player have enough gold?”) a plain IF remains the right and clearer choice.
Ein klassischer Einsatz: Du liest Text e: A classic use: you read text in and want to make a number of it. Rather than building TRY/CATCH around VAL, TRYVAL(text, ersatz) (chapter “Strings”) is often the simpler solution here — on invalid input it quietly supplies a fallback value. Reach for TRY/CATCH when there is no such convenient safety net.
Eine gewöhnliche Funktion läuft von oben: An ordinary function runs from the top to its RETURN and is then finished. A coroutine can do more: it may halt in mid-execution, hand a value to the outside — and later carry on at exactly the point where it stopped. It remembers its complete state while doing so: every local variable, the place in the code, everything. Picture it as a function with a pause button.
Das klingt exotisch, ist aber für Spiele: That sounds exotic, but for games it is worth its weight in gold: cutscenes that play out step by step; enemy patterns that do this for a while and then that; or generating an endless sequence of numbers, value by value. This chapter is demanding — take your time and try the examples out yourself.
Was eine Coroutine zur Coroutine macht: What makes a coroutine a coroutine
Du brauchst kein besonderes Schlüsselwor: You need no special keyword in the definition. As soon as a YIELD appears anywhere in the body of a FUNCTION (or SUB), it is automatically a coroutine. YIELD means “stop here and hand this value to the outside”.
Und jetzt das Überraschende: Rufst du ei: And now the surprising part: when you call a coroutine, its code does not run AT ALL to begin with. Instead you get back a handle — a kind of remote control for the paused coroutine, which you keep in a variable of type COROUTINE. Only CORO_RESUME starts and drives it.
YIELD hält die Coroutine an und gibt ein: YIELD halts the coroutine and hands a value outward. CORO_RESUME carries it on to the next YIELD and delivers that value. If the coroutine finishes during this step, CORO_RESUME delivers its RETURN value instead.
startet NICHT – liefert ein Handle: does NOT start - gives back a handle
läuft zu Ende: der RETURN-Wert: runs to the end: the RETURN value
Jeder CORO_RESUME nimmt den Faden dort w: Every CORO_RESUME picks the thread up where the last YIELD dropped it. The coroutine remembers everything in between.
Ist sie fertig? CORO_DONE und CORO_RESUL: Is it finished? CORO_DONE and CORO_RESULT
Mit CORO_DONE fragst du, ob eine Corouti: With CORO_DONE you ask whether a coroutine has run through. You can then collect its final RETURN value at any time with CORO_RESULT.
CORO_DONE liefert TRUE, sobald die Corou: CORO_DONE gives TRUE once the coroutine has finished. CORO_RESULT gives its final RETURN value (only meaningful once it is done).
jetzt läuft sie zu Ende: now it runs to the end
Willst du einfach nur alle Werte einsamm: If you simply want to collect all the values a coroutine spits out one after another, you do not have to juggle RESUME and DONE yourself. FOR EACH drives the coroutine to the end automatically and hands you every value delivered. That is the clearest way to walk a generating coroutine (a “generator”).

Treibe eine UNENDLICHE Coroutine (eine o: Never drive an ENDLESS coroutine (one with no natural end) with FOR EACH — that runs for ever. Steer it by hand with CORO_RESUME instead and break off yourself once you have enough values. Tip: in a manual RESUME loop the very last (finishing) call delivers the RETURN value or NIL — so for plain collecting, FOR EACH is the safer choice.
YIELD ist keine Einbahnstraße. YIELD ist: YIELD is not a one-way street. YIELD is itself an expression: you can assign its result to a variable. With CORO_SEND you not only carry the coroutine on but push a value into it as you do — and that value becomes the result of the YIELD at which it is currently paused. A genuine dialogue between your code and the coroutine arises that way.
Setzt die Coroutine fort wie CORO_RESUME: Carries the coroutine on like CORO_RESUME, but the YIELD expression at which it is paused delivers the value passed in. (At the very first start there is no waiting YIELD yet — use CORO_RESUME there.)
x bekommt den hineingegebenen Wert: x receives the value passed in
Coroutinen sind ein Spezialwerkzeug – fü: Coroutines are a specialist tool — for many programs you will never need them. Where they do fit, though, they simplify the code enormously, because the coroutine keeps track of its own progress instead of your having to carry it laboriously in variables:
Zwischensequenzen / Dialoge: ein Schritt: Cutscenes and dialogue: one step per YIELD, the rest waits.
Gegner- oder Boss-Muster: „fahre links,: Enemy or boss patterns: “move left, wait, fire three times, from the top.”
Generatoren: erzeuge eine (auch endlose): Generators: produce a sequence of values on demand — an endless one, if you like.
Eine pausierte Coroutine, die du nicht z: A paused coroutine that you do not let run to the end can be shut down cleanly with CORO_CLOSE(c). In short programs that is rarely necessary; with many long-lived coroutines it is good form.
Je größer ein Programm wird, desto unhan: The bigger a program grows, the more unwieldy a single enormous file becomes. With IMPORT you pull in code from outside — either one of Drachenhauch's many built-in libraries or a file of your own into which you have moved reusable code. That keeps your programs tidy and saves typing, because you do not keep rewriting what already works.
Eine IMPORT-Zeile schreibst du an den An: You write an IMPORT line at the start of your program. There are two sorts of module, and they differ in one small detail — remember that difference well.
Drachenhauch bringt eine große Sammlung: Drachenhauch ships a large collection of ready-made modules — for 2D vectors, JSON, databases, physics, pathfinding and much more (you will meet them all in Part V). You fetch such a module with IMPORT and the module name in quotation marks, WITHOUT a file extension. Afterwards the module's functions and types are at your disposal.
Macht ein eingebautes Modul nutzbar. Der: Makes a built-in module usable. The name goes in quotation marks with no extension. Afterwards you can use the module's functions and external types.
Du kannst deinen eigenen Code in eine se: You can move your own code into a separate .dh file and import it. That divides a large program into manageable pieces — all the maths helpers in mathe.dh, for instance. When importing a file of your own you give the file name WITH the .dh extension. Drachenhauch inserts the file's contents at that point, so you can use its functions and constants directly.

Fügt den Inhalt einer eigenen .dh-Datei: Inserts the contents of one of your own .dh files — given with its extension, relative to your program's directory. Afterwards its functions, SUBs, classes and constants are available.
Hier der feine, aber wichtige Unterschie: Here is the fine but important difference: you write a built-in module WITHOUT an extension (IMPORT "vec2") and a file of your own WITH one (IMPORT "mathe.dh"). The .dh extension tells Drachenhauch: “this is a file of mine, not a built-in module.”
Manche Module haben lange Funktionsnamen: Some modules have long function names. With the addition AS you give a module a shorter name prefix on import. The JSON functions, which normally begin with JSON_, then become J_ functions, say — which saves typing when you use the module often.
Importiert ein Modul und ersetzt sein Na: Imports a module and replaces its name prefix with the abbreviation given. JSON_PARSE thus becomes J_PARSE, for example.
Der Alias ersetzt das Präfix für alle Fu: The alias replaces the prefix for all the module's functions and types (J_PARSE, J_HANDLE …). It works for modules whose functions begin with the module name — that is, for the great majority.
Lagere zusammengehörige Bausteine in eig: Move related building blocks into files of their own: one for maths helpers, one for your player class, one for the enemies. Your main program then begins with a few IMPORT lines and stays readable. That way you find your bearings even in large projects — and can simply reuse a file that has proved itself in your next game.
